title: Jane Street Suffers Record $15 Billion Loss From AI Selloff and Hedge Fund Blowup
excerpt: The Wall Street trading giant's worst monthly loss ever was driven by the collapse of AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness and a broader tech stock rout, though the firm still boasts $40 billion in year-to-date revenue.
body:
• Jane Street lost approximately $15 billion in July — its worst monthly loss ever — driven by the AI stock selloff and the collapse of hedge fund Situational Awareness
  • Jane Street's $2.5 billion investment in Situational Awareness had grown to nearly $10 billion before crashing to $3-3.5 billion, accounting for roughly $7 billion of the loss
  • Despite the record loss, Jane Street has generated more than $40 billion in trading revenue year-to-date, outstripping every major Wall Street bank
  • Situational Awareness founder Leopold Aschenbrenner was forced to sell the bulk of his stock portfolio to Ken Griffin's Citadel in a fire sale after margin calls

Jane Street, one of Wall Street's most formidable and secretive trading firms, suffered its worst monthly loss on record in July — approximately $15 billion — as an AI-focused stock selloff ripped through its portfolio and cratered its investment in hedge fund Situational Awareness, according to the Wall Street Journal and Reuters.

The staggering loss is a rare stumble for a firm renowned for its risk management discipline. Yet it comes in the context of what remains Jane Street's best trading year ever, with revenues exceeding $40 billion through July — a figure that dwarfs the trading performance of every major Wall Street bank.

The Situational Awareness Collapse

The largest single driver of Jane Street's losses was its unusually large outside bet on Situational Awareness, a hedge fund led by Leopold Aschenbrenner, a former OpenAI researcher who built a $45 billion firm at the center of the AI investment boom.

Jane Street originally invested $2.5 billion in Situational Awareness — an unusual move for a firm that rarely allocates capital to outside managers. The stake soared to nearly $10 billion as AI stocks surged in the first half of 2026. But when the AI selloff hit in July, Aschenbrenner's aggressive, leverage-fueled bets turned toxic.

"They had a large drawdown that left our stake about flat on the year, but still up over the entire period we have been invested."

— Jane Street internal note to employees, as seen by Reuters

The investment collapsed to between $3 billion and $3.5 billion — a loss of nearly $7 billion. Facing margin calls, Aschenbrenner was forced to offload the bulk of Situational's stock portfolio in what sources described as a fire sale to billionaire Ken Griffin's Citadel.

Broader AI and Asia Losses

The remaining $8 billion in losses came from Jane Street's own positions. In its note to employees, the firm said it "largely lost on the same portfolio of trades that had strong outperformance in the second quarter." Several of the largest memory and semiconductor stocks fell roughly 50% during July.

The firm also took hits on long positions in non-AI stocks in Asia, where many quant trading firms suffered during the month. Trades in China were particularly painful across the quantitative trading industry.

Jane Street said it has since "closed a significant portion of our risk in the specific areas we lost on in July" and has "reduced risk taking in other strategies" going forward.

A Firm in Transition

The loss exposes how deeply Jane Street has woven itself into the AI trade. The firm, founded 26 years ago with a handful of employees, now employs 3,500 people and plans to recruit more than 500 this year. In April, it struck a deal to invest $1 billion in AI computing company CoreWeave and spend $6 billion to use its AI cloud platform.

That strategic pivot toward AI — both as a trading thesis and a business tool — means the firm's fortunes are increasingly tied to the sector's volatile swings.

What It Means for Markets

The episode underscores the concentration risk building across Wall Street's AI bets. When Situational Awareness was forced to liquidate, the ripple effects hit not just Jane Street but the broader market, as forced selling accelerated the decline in AI-related equities.

For investors tracking AI sector exposure, the Jane Street episode is a warning: even the most sophisticated risk managers on Wall Street can be caught on the wrong side of a crowded trade when sentiment shifts. The firm's decision to pull back risk signals that the era of unlimited AI exuberance among institutional investors may be cooling.
